I fixed `slugify()`, and all 4 tests pass (the old one plus the new ones I added).

`src/util/slug.ts` now:

```ts
export function slugify(title: string): string {
  return title
    .normalize("NFKD")
    .replace(/\p{M}/gu, "")
    .toLowerCase()
    .replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, "-")
    .replace(/^-+|-+$/g, "");
}
```

- **Accents:** `normalize("NFKD")` splits letters like `é` into a plain `e` plus a separate accent mark, and `\p{M}` then removes the marks. `'Café Déjà Vu'` becomes `'cafe-deja-vu'`.
- **Allowed characters:** any run of characters that aren't `a-z` or `0-9` becomes a single dash. `'Hello, World!'` becomes `'hello-world'`.
- **Ends:** dashes at the start and end are removed.

The new tests in `test/slug.test.ts` cover the accent example, repeated spaces and punctuation, dashes at both ends, `'Version 2.0'` → `'version-2-0'`, and `'!!!'` → `''`.

Two things to be aware of:
- A title with no letters or digits, like `'!!!'`, now gives an empty slug. If slugs are used in URLs or as IDs, you may want a fallback for that case.
- Letters that aren't accented versions of a–z are dropped, not converted. For example, `ß` and `ø` disappear, and Cyrillic, Greek or CJK titles come out empty. Proper transliteration would need a library. Say if you want it.

I fixed `addMonths()`. `addMonths('2026-01-31', 1)` now returns `'2026-02-28'`, and the full test suite passes (6 pass, 0 fail).

**The cause:** `setUTCMonth` keeps the day of the month. Asking for "February 31" rolls over into March, which is how you got `'2026-03-03'`.

**The fix** (`src/util/months.ts`):
- It counts months as one running total across years (year × 12 + month), adds the offset, then splits the result back into a year and month. Negative counts and year ends need no special handling that way.
- It finds the last day of the target month using day 0 of the following month. That gets leap years right without any special code.
- It uses whichever is smaller: the original day or that last day.

**New tests** in `test/months.test.ts`:
- Leap years: `2028-01-31 +1 → 2028-02-29` and `2024-02-29 +12 → 2025-02-28`.
- Year ends: `2026-11-30 +3 → 2027-02-28`.
- Negative counts: `2026-03-31 -1 → 2026-02-28` and `2026-05-15 -17 → 2024-12-15`.
- Days that already fit stay the same.

for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i += size) out.push(items.slice(i, i + size));

- **404** `{ "error": "user not found" }` when the id is valid but no user has it.
- **200** with the user object for real users, same as before.

One thing to know: `/users/007` is treated as user 7 instead of being rejected. If you'd rather reject leading zeros, change the regex to `/^[1-9]\d*$/`.

**What was wrong** (`src/users.ts`): `parseInt` accepts a lot more than you'd expect. It reads `"12x"` as 12 and `"1.5"` as 1, and turns `"abc"` into `NaN`. Then the handler sent back `null` with a 200 for any id it didn't find.

**What changed:**
- **400** `{ "error": "user id must be a positive whole number" }` for any id that isn't all digits or is less than 1. That covers `abc`, `0`, `1.5`, `12x`, `-1`, `1e2` and an empty id (`/users/`). It also covers ids too large to be stored exactly as a number, like `99999999999999999999`.
- **404** `{ "error": "user not found" }` for a valid id with no matching user.
- **200** for real users, with the same body as before (e.g. `{"id":1,"name":"Ada"}`).

**Tests** (`test/users.test.ts`): I added a test that a real user still comes back the same, a check that the 404 has the error body, and a 400 test for each bad id listed above.

**Decision for you:** ids with leading zeros, like `/users/01`, are accepted and treated as user 1. If you'd rather those get a 400, the pattern just needs to change to `/^[1-9]\d*$/`.

turns.reply_text:
I fixed it: `'1h30m'` now gives 5400. I added tests to `test/duration.test.ts` and the full suite passes (`bun test`: 5 pass, 0 fail).

**The bug:** `parseDuration()` used an unanchored regex that found only the first number-and-unit pair. So `'1h30m'` read just the `1h`. Because it didn't need to match the whole string, it also accepted junk like `'10m please'`.

**The fix** (`src/util/duration.ts`): the regex `^(?:(\d+)h)?(?:(\d+)m)?(?:(\d+)s)?$` now has to match the entire string. Hours, minutes and seconds are each optional, at most once, in h, m, s order, and their values are added up. Since every part is optional, an empty string would also match, so there's an explicit check that throws in that case.

**What the tests cover:**
- **Valid input:** single units (`90s`, `5m`, `2h`), all three (`2h5m10s` → 7510) and a gap in the middle (`1h10s` → 3610).
- **Input that must throw:** `''`, `'5x'`, `'10m please'`, `'abc'`, units out of order (`'30m1h'`), a repeated unit (`'5m5m'`), a unit with no number (`'h'`), decimals (`'1.5h'`) and a leading space.

Two behaviours you might not expect: decimals like `'1.5h'` are rejected, and so are spaces anywhere in the string. Both follow from your spec, but if callers might pass padded strings, you'd want to trim before parsing.

turns.reply_text:
I fixed `parseDuration()` in `src/util/duration.ts`. `'1h30m'` now gives 5400, and `'2h5m10s'` gives 7510. The full test suite passes.

**The bug:** the old regex had no anchors and wasn't global. It matched only the first number-and-unit pair it found and ignored everything else. So `'1h30m'` became 3600, and `'10m please'` returned 600 instead of throwing.

**The fix:** one anchored pattern, `/^(?:(\d+)h)?(?:(\d+)m)?(?:(\d+)s)?$/`. It has an optional group for each unit, in h, m, s order. The anchors mean the whole string has to match, so these all throw now:
- an unknown unit (`'5x'`)
- extra text before or after (`'10m please'`, `' 5m'`)
- units out of order (`'30m1h'`) or repeated (`'1h1h'`)
- a unit with no number (`'h'`) or a decimal (`'1.5h'`)

Every group is optional, so the pattern also matches an empty string. There's an explicit check that makes `''` throw too.

I added tests to `test/duration.test.ts` for single units, all three units together, and the invalid inputs above.

Two edge cases you might not expect: values that don't fit the usual range are accepted (`'90m'` gives 5400), and so is `'0s'`. You didn't mention either, so I left them allowed.

I checked GBrain first, as your instructions ask, but it had nothing about this project.
